parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by the *amplitude modulation* (AM) of a radio wave.

markscheme_points.text: amplitude of the high-frequency carrier wave is varied
in synchrony / accordance with the displacement of the information (audio) signal

hints: Hint 1: Think about the two waves involved - a high frequency carrier that does the travelling and a low frequency audio signal that carries the sound information. Which one does the listening, and which one is changed?
Hint 2: Focus on what happens to the size of the carrier oscillations as the audio signal goes up and down, and remember what stays constant for AM - amplitude or frequency?
parts.proper_answer: The amplitude of the high-frequency carrier wave is varied in accordance with the displacement of the audio (information) signal. The carrier frequency remains constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate the two roles**
You have a fast carrier radio wave that can travel far, and a slow audio wave that contains the music or speech. The carrier itself carries no information until you impress the audio onto it.

Step 2: **What AM changes**
In AM the loudness pattern of the sound is copied onto the height of the carrier. So $$A_{carrier} \text{ varies with } x_{audio}$$ where $A$ is amplitude and $x$ is displacement. When the audio displacement is large, the carrier peaks are tall, and when it is small the carrier peaks are short. The frequency of the carrier does not change.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State two advantages of AM transmissions when compared with frequency modulation (FM) transmissions.

markscheme_points.text: greater range / each transmitter covers a greater distance (fewer transmitters needed)
smaller bandwidth allows more stations to share waveband (and cheaper transmitters/receivers)

hints: Hint 1: Compare how much frequency space each type needs and how far each type can reach, especially at long and medium wavelengths.
Hint 2: Think about the receiver and transmitter circuits - which system needs simpler electronics and therefore costs less to build?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Smaller bandwidth required so more stations can be accommodated in a given frequency range. 2. Greater range / larger area of reception for same power, and simpler cheaper transmitter and receiver circuits.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Bandwidth and stations**
An AM transmission occupies a narrow band of frequencies, about twice the highest audio frequency. An FM transmission needs a much wider band. That means you can fit many more AM stations into the medium-wave band.

Step 2: **Range and cost**
AM uses long and medium wavelengths that diffract round hills and reflect from the ionosphere, so one transmitter covers a very large area. The modulation and demodulation circuits are also much simpler and cheaper than for FM. The price you pay is lower sound quality and more interference.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: the wavelength of the carrier wave
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 5.1 and pick out the tall central line - that marks the carrier frequency in kHz. Remember all radio waves travel through air at the same speed as light in free space.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the carrier frequency**
The tall line in the centre of Fig. 5.1 is the carrier. It is at $$f = 1500\text{ kHz} = 1.5 \times 10^{6}\text{ Hz}$$

Step 2: **Convert to wavelength**
Radio waves are electromagnetic waves with $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Use $$c = f\lambda$$ $$\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{8}}{1.5 \times 10^{6}} = 200\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the maximum frequency of the transmitted audio signal.
hints: Hint 1: Look at how far the spread of frequencies extends on either side of the 1500 kHz carrier in Fig. 5.1. That sideband width equals the highest audio frequency present.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link sideband width to audio**
AM creates an upper sideband $f_c + f_{audio}$ and a lower sideband $f_c - f_{audio}$. So the total spread is twice the highest audio frequency.

Step 2: **Read the edge**
From Fig. 5.1 the upper edge is at $1510\text{ kHz}$ and the carrier $f_c$ is at $1500\text{ kHz}$. Hence $$f_{audio,max} = 1510 - 1500 = 10\text{ kHz}$$ The lower edge at $1490\text{ kHz}$ confirms the same $10\text{ kHz}$ width.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
Another audio signal with the same maximum frequency is transmitted using a different carrier wave frequency. The lowest frequency of this modulated wave is equal to the highest frequency of the modulated wave in (b).

Determine the frequency of this carrier wave.
hints: Hint 1: For the new station, its lowest transmitted frequency is carrier minus the maximum audio frequency from (b)(ii). Set that equal to the old highest frequency and solve for the new carrier.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the sideband rule for the new carrier**
Let the new carrier be $f_{c,new}$. With the same $f_{audio,max} = 10\text{ kHz}$, its lowest frequency is $$f_{low,new} = f_{c,new} - 10\text{ kHz}$$

Step 2: **Match to the old top edge**
The old highest frequency from (b) is $1510\text{ kHz}$. You are told $$f_{low,new} = 1510\text{ kHz}$$ so $$f_{c,new} - 10 = 1510$$ $$f_{c,new} = 1520\text{ kHz}$$ This places the two $20\text{ kHz}$ wide bands side by side with no overlap.
